claim: Metabolites downstream of adenylosuccinate lyase occur at lower concentrations in humans compared to chimpanzees and macaques.
source: Although several compounds in amino acid metabolism occur at either higher or lower concentrations in humans than in the other primates, metabolites downstream of adenylosuccinate lyase, which catalyzes two reactions in purine synthesis, occur at lower concentrations in humans.
evidence: Supported by CE-MS measurements showing lower concentrations of metabolites downstream of ADSL in human tissues compared to other primates

claim: Adenylosuccinate lyase carries an amino acid substitution (A429V) that is present in all humans today but absent in Neandertals.
source: This enzyme carries an amino acid substitution that is present in all humans today but absent in Neandertals.
evidence: Supported by genomic sequence data from modern humans and Neandertals

claim: The A429V amino acid substitution in ADSL contributes to much or all of the reduction of de novo synthesis of purines in humans.
source: By introducing the modern human substitution into the genomes of mice, as well as the ancestral, Neandertal-like substitution into the genomes of human cells, we show that this amino acid substitution contributes to much or all of the reduction of de novo synthesis of purines in humans.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from humanized mice and ancestralized human cells showing changes in purine biosynthesis

claim: Modern humans differ dramatically from their closest evolutionary relatives in a number of ways.
source: Modern humans differ dramatically from their closest evolutionary relatives in a number of ways.
evidence: Based on established scientific knowledge about human evolution

claim: Modern humans have developed rapidly changing and complex cultures that have allowed them to become more numerous and widespread than any other primates and closely related hominins such as Neandertals.
source: Most strikingly, they have developed rapidly changing and complex cultures that have allowed them to become more numerous and widespread than any other primates and closely related hominins such as Neandertals.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about human cultural evolution and population expansion

claim: It has proven difficult to identify the genetic and biological underpinnings of traits unique to humans.
source: However, although large numbers of traits have been identified as being unique to humans or been suggested to be so (e.g. Tomasello, 2019, Varki and Altheide, 2005), it has proven difficult to identify the genetic and biological underpinnings of such traits.
evidence: Supported by citations to previous research on human-specific traits

claim: Many human-specific traits are genetically complex.
source: One reason may be that many of them are genetically complex (Phillips, 2008) and represent differences in degree rather than absolute differences between humans and other groups.
evidence: Supported by citation to Phillips, 2008

claim: About one hundred protein-coding genes carry amino acid substitutions that are fixed or almost fixed in present-day humans but occur in their ancestral state in Neandertals and Denisovans.
source: The gene encoding ADSL in humans is located on chromosome 22q13.1–13.2 and is one of only approximately one hundred protein-coding genes that carry substitutions inferred to change amino acids that are fixed or almost fixed in present-day humans but occur in their ancestral, ape-like state in the genomes of the closest extinct relatives of modern humans, Neandertals and Denisovans (Pääbo, 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Pääbo, 2014

claim: The ADSL substitution in modern humans is an alanine to valine substitution at position 429 (A429V).
source: The substitution in ADSL in modern humans is an alanine to valine substitution at position 429 (A429V).
evidence: Supported by genomic sequence data

claim: Neandertals, Denisovans, all other primates and most mammals carry an alanine residue at position 429 of ADSL.
source: Neandertals, Denisovans, all other primates and most mammals carry an alanine residue at this position (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3

claim: The A429V substitution is located in a protein domain that forms part of the substrate channel over the active site of the enzyme.
source: The substitution is located in a protein domain that forms part of the substrate channel over the active site of the enzyme.
evidence: Based on structural analysis of ADSL protein

claim: Amino acid substitutions close to position 429 in ADSL cause lowered enzymatic activity and/or lower enzyme stability and result in symptoms that include psychomotor retardation, autism, and epilepsy.
source: Amino acid substitutions close to this position cause lowered enzymatic activity and/or lower enzyme stability and result in symptoms that include psychomotor retardation, autism, and epilepsy (Jurecka et al., 2015; Spiegel et al., 2006; Zikanova et al., 2010) as well as alterations in brain structure as seen by magnetic resonance imaging (Jurecka et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to clinical studies

claim: In wild-type adult mice, mean ADSL activity varied from 1.95 nmole/min/μg in liver to 24.4 nmole/min/μg in muscle.
source: In the wild-type adult mice (n = 10), mean ADSL activity varied from 1.95 nmole/min/μg in liver to 24.4 nmole/min/μg in muscle (Figure 4b).
evidence: Supported by enzymatic activity measurements shown in Figure 4b

claim: In humanized mice, ADSL activity was reduced by 8.7% to 56% in all organs in both adults and pups.
source: In the humanized mice, ADSL activity was reduced by 8.7% to 56% in all organs in both adults (n = 11) and pups (n = 12) (Figure 4; p<0.05, for all comparisons in both age groups).
evidence: Supported by enzymatic activity measurements shown in Figure 4

claim: The relative reduction of ADSL activity in humanized mice is higher in cerebral cortex (43% in pups and 56% in adults) than in other tissues (8.7%–40%).
source: The relative reduction of the activity in the humanized relative to the wild-type mice is higher in cerebral cortex (43% in pups and 56% in adults) than in the other tissues (8.7%–40%).
evidence: Supported by enzymatic activity measurements in different tissues

claim: 36 metabolites showed significant concentration differences in cerebellum of 12-week-old humanized mice compared to wild-type.
source: According to this test, 36 metabolites showed significant concentration differences in cerebellum of 12-week-old mice (permutation test, p=0.036) and 45 metabolites showed marginally significant differences in the cerebral cortex of 1-week-old mice (permutation test, p=0.081, Supplementary file 9).
evidence: Supported by GC-MS metabolomic measurements and statistical analysis

claim: The metabolic effects of the two mutations introduced in ADSL are particularly pronounced in the central nervous system.
source: Thus, the metabolic effects of the two mutations introduced in ADSL are particularly pronounced in the central nervous system.
evidence: Inferred from metabolomic data showing significant differences primarily in brain tissues

claim: Six metabolites within the purine biosynthesis pathway were detected in 12-week-old mice.
source: In the 12-week-old mice, we detected six metabolites within the purine biosynthesis pathway.
evidence: Supported by GC-MS metabolomic measurements

claim: In humanized mice, four purine biosynthesis metabolites had lower concentrations than in wild-type mice in cerebral cortex and all six had lower concentrations in cerebellum.
source: In the humanized mice, four of these metabolites had lower concentrations than in the wild-type mice in the cerebral cortex and all of them had lower concentrations in the cerebellum (binomial test for cortex and cerebellum, p=0.04) (Figure 5b).
evidence: Supported by metabolomic data shown in Figure 5b

claim: Concentrations of all six purine biosynthesis metabolites were significantly lower in the cerebellum of 12-week-old humanized mice compared to metabolites assigned to other metabolic pathways.
source: Further, concentrations of all six purine biosynthesis metabolites were significantly lower in the cerebellum of 12-week-old mice compared to metabolites assigned to other metabolic pathways (Wilcoxon test, p=0.04; Figure 5c).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of metabolomic data shown in Figure 5c

claim: The A429V substitution does not affect the kinetics of the murine ADSL enzyme.
source: In summary, the A429V substitution does not affect the kinetics of the murine ADSL enzyme.
evidence: Supported by enzyme kinetics measurements shown in Figure 6a

claim: The A429V substitution decreases the secondary structure stability of the ADSL protein.
source: However, it decreases the secondary structure stability of the protein.
evidence: Supported by circular dichroism measurements shown in Figure 6b

claim: Mouse ADSL protein with alanine at position 429 was more stable (50% folded at 68.3°C) than mouse ADSL protein with valine at position 429 (50% folded at 67.9°C).
source: Mouse ADSL protein with alanine at position 429 was more stable (50% folded at 68.3°C,±0.2°C, n = 5) than mouse ADSL protein with valine at position 429 (50% folded at 67.9°C ± 0.2°C, n = 5).
evidence: Supported by circular dichroism thermal denaturation measurements

claim: No differences in specific activity between the human and Neandertal versions of ADSL were detected using either SAMP or SAICAR as substrate.
source: No differences in specific activity between the two enzymes were detected using either substrate (SAMP, t-test, p=0.41 or SAICAR, t-test, p=0.81, Figure 7a).
evidence: Supported by enzyme kinetics measurements shown in Figure 7a

claim: The conversion of SAICAR to AICAR is reduced about 1.8-fold for the modern human form of ADSL in the presence of both substrates while the ancestral form shows no reduction.
source: In contrast, the conversion of SAICAR to AICAR is reduced about 1.8-fold for the modern human form in the presence of both substrates (p=0.026) while the ancestral form of the enzyme shows no reduction (p=0.44; Figure 7c).
evidence: Supported by enzyme kinetics measurements with mixed substrates shown in Figure 7c

claim: The temperature at which 50% of the protein is inferred to be folded is 67.0°C for the modern human form of ADSL and 68.0°C for the Neandertal-like form.
source: The temperature at which 50% of the protein is inferred to be folded is 67.0°C (± SEM = 0.10°C) for the modern human form of the protein and 68.0°C (± SEM = 0.2°C) for the Neandertal-like form of the protein (Figure 8a).
evidence: Supported by circular dichroism thermal denaturation measurements shown in Figure 8a

claim: Modern human ADSL is less stable than ancestral ADSL.
source: Thus, as previously shown (Van Laer et al., 2018), modern human ADSL is less stable than ancestral ADSL.
evidence: Supported by circular dichroism measurements and previous publication

claim: At 1.0125 M GdnHCl about 50% of the modern human version of ADSL was present as tetramers whereas for the ancestral form this was the case at 1.125 M GdnHCl.
source: Figure 8b shows that at 1.0125 M GdnHCl about 50% of the modern human version of ADSL was present as tetramers whereas for the ancestral form this was the case at 1.125 M GdnHCl.
evidence: Supported by native gel electrophoresis measurements shown in Figure 8b

claim: Both the secondary and quaternary structures of the ancestral form of ADSL are more stable than for the modern human form.
source: Thus, both the secondary and quaternary structures of the ancestral form of ADSL are more stable than for the modern human form.
evidence: Supported by circular dichroism and native gel electrophoresis measurements

claim: Out of 10 detected metabolites downstream of ADSL, all but one (adenine) have lower concentrations in wild type human cells compared to cells carrying the V429A substitution.
source: Strikingly, out of 10 detected metabolites downstream of ADSL, all but one (adenine) have lower concentrations in the wild type cells (binom. test, p=0.01; Wilcoxon test, p=0.06, Figure 9a).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS metabolomic measurements shown in Figure 9a

claim: In human cells, the ancestral form of ADSL supports a higher level of purine biosynthesis than the modern human form.
source: Thus, in human cells, the ancestral form of ADSL supports a higher level of purine biosynthesis than the modern human form.
evidence: Inferred from metabolomic data comparing wild-type and ancestralized human cells

claim: Four purine biosynthesis metabolites (guanosine, inosine, hypoxanthine, xanthine) are present at lower levels in human cells compared to chimpanzee cells.
source: Out of 1883 metabolite peaks that differ significantly (Wilcoxon test, BH-adjusted p<0.05) between the human and chimpanzee wild-type cells, four correspond to purine biosynthesis metabolites (guanosine, inosine, hypoxanthine, xanthine) and are present at lower levels in human cells compared to chimpanzee cells.
evidence: Supported by LC-MS metabolomic measurements comparing human and chimpanzee cells

claim: Seven out of ten purine biosynthesis metabolites are present in lower amounts in human cells compared to chimpanzee cells.
source: Seven of them are present in lower amounts in the human cells (Figure 9a) and as a group they are present in lower concentrations in the human than in the chimpanzee cells when compared to metabolites in other pathways (Wilcox test, p=0.01, Figure 9b).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS metabolomic measurements shown in Figure 9

claim: Six of the 10 purine biosynthesis metabolites are present at significantly lower concentrations in humans than in macaques.
source: Six of the 10 purine biosynthesis metabolites are present at significantly lower concentrations in humans than in macaques when analyzed individually (Figure 9a) and as a group they are present at lower concentrations than metabolites in other pathways (Wilcoxon test, p=0.04, Figure 9b).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS metabolomic measurements shown in Figure 9

claim: Reversal of the A429V substitution in ADSL in human cells results in an increase in purine biosynthesis similar in magnitude to what is observed when chimpanzee cells are compared to human cells.
source: Thus, reversal of the A429V substitution in ADSL in human cells results in an increase in purine biosynthesis similar in magnitude to what is observed when chimpanzee cells are compared to human cells.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of metabolomic data from ancestralized human cells and chimpanzee cells

claim: The ancestors of modern humans diverged from their closest evolutionary relatives, Neandertals and Denisovans, on the order of 600,000 years ago.
source: The ancestors of modern humans diverged from their closest evolutionary relatives, Neandertals and Denisovans, on the order of 600,000 years ago (Prüfer et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Prüfer et al., 2014

claim: The ancestors of hominins diverged from the ancestors of chimpanzees and bonobos about 6 million years ago.
source: About 10 times further back the ancestors of hominins diverged from the ancestors of chimpanzees and bonobos (Langergraber et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citation to Langergraber et al., 2012 and calculation from 600,000 years

claim: For about 90% of the genome, Neandertals and Denisovans fall within the variation of present-day humans.
source: In contrast, modern humans and Neandertals and Denisovans diverged so recently that for about 90% of the genome, the two archaic human groups fall within the variation of present-day humans (Green et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citation to Green et al., 2010

claim: When modern and archaic humans met about 50,000 years ago, they interbred.
source: Furthermore, when modern and archaic humans met about 50,000 years ago, they interbred.
evidence: Based on established knowledge about human-Neandertal interbreeding

claim: Neandertal DNA fragments that together make up about half of the Neandertal genome exist in present-day humans.
source: This resulted in that Neandertal DNA fragments that together make up about half of the Neandertal genome exist in present-day humans (Sankararaman et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Sankararaman et al., 2014

claim: Position 429 in ADSL is conserved as alanine in most tetrapods.
source: Position 429 is conserved as alanine in most tetrapods suggesting that it may be of importance.
evidence: Based on sequence conservation analysis across tetrapods

claim: An arginine to histidine substitution at position 426 in ADSL causes the most common form of adenylosuccinase deficiency in present-day humans.
source: Position 429 is also located only three positions away from position 426, where an arginine to histidine substitution causes the most common form of adenylosuccinase deficiency in present-day humans (Edery et al., 2003; Kmoch, 2000; Maaswinkel-Mooij et al., 1997; Marie et al., 1999; Race et al., 2000).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to clinical studies

claim: A genomic region centered around ADSL is among the top 20 candidate regions that have experienced selective sweeps in humans after their split from Neandertals but before the separation of Africans and Eurasians.
source: Further evidence suggesting that a change in ADSL may have been of importance in the evolution of modern humans comes from a screen for genomic regions that have experienced selective sweeps in humans after their split from Neandertals but before the separation of Africans and Eurasians (Racimo, 2016). In that study, a genomic region centered around ADSL is among the top 20 candidate regions, although it also contains other genes.
evidence: Supported by citation to Racimo, 2016

claim: The A429V substitution in ADSL may have contributed to human-specific changes in brain development and function.
source: Although no overt morphological or other brain-related phenotypes are observed in the mice humanized at pos. 428 and 429 (data not shown), it is thus possible that the A429V substitution in ADSL has contributed to human-specific changes in brain development and function.
evidence: Speculative statement based on observed metabolic changes in brain

claim: 22 metabolites have higher concentrations in human cerebellum compared to chimpanzees and macaques, with 18 of them being amino acids.
source: In cerebellum, 22 metabolites have higher concentrations in humans whereas no metabolites have lower concentrations (Supplementary file 2). Eighteen of the 22 metabolites are amino acids.
evidence: Supported by CE-MS metabolomic measurements

claim: Five metabolites have lower concentrations in human prefrontal cortex compared to chimpanzees and macaques, with three being purines (IMP, GMP, AMP) and two being NAD+ and UDP-N-acetylglucosamine.
source: In prefrontal cortex, we detected five metabolites with lower concentrations in humans and none with higher concentrations (Supplementary file 3). Three of the five metabolites are purines (inosine monophosphate [IMP], guanosine monophosphate [GMP], adenosine monophosphate [AMP]) and the other two are NAD+ and UDP-N-acetylglucosamine.
evidence: Supported by CE-MS metabolomic measurements

claim: Between 8 and 12 pathways are associated with higher metabolite concentrations in the five human tissues analyzed.
source: Between 8 and 12 pathways are associated with higher metabolite concentrations in the five human tissues (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: Supported by KEGG pathway analysis of metabolomic data

claim: All eight pathways identified in the prefrontal cortex with higher metabolite concentrations involve amino acid metabolism.
source: All eight pathways identified in the prefrontal cortex involve amino acid metabolism, eight out of nine pathways in the visual cortex and nine out of 10 in the cerebellum also involve amino acids.
evidence: Supported by KEGG pathway analysis of metabolomic data

claim: Several aspects of amino acid metabolism seem to be increased in humans relative to other primates.
source: Thus, several aspects of amino acid metabolism seem to be increased in humans relative to other primates.
evidence: Inferred from pathway analysis showing multiple amino acid pathways with higher metabolite concentrations

claim: Oxidative phosphorylation shows decreased metabolite concentrations in the three brain regions analyzed in humans.
source: One of these pathways is oxidative phosphorylation, which shows decreased metabolite concentrations in the three brain regions.
evidence: Supported by metabolomic data and pathway analysis

claim: Oxidative phosphorylation is not affected in muscle and kidneys.
source: Because oxidative phosphorylation is not affected in muscle and kidneys, it seems that the human brain differs from ape brains in that oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria is less active.
evidence: Supported by metabolomic data showing no differences in muscle and kidney

claim: The human brain differs from ape brains in that oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria is less active.
source: Because oxidative phosphorylation is not affected in muscle and kidneys, it seems that the human brain differs from ape brains in that oxidative phosphorylation in mitochondria is less active.
evidence: Inferred from tissue-specific differences in oxidative phosphorylation metabolites

claim: Purine biosynthesis is decreased in humans relative to apes in the brain as well as in other organs based on KEGG pathway definition.
source: Based on the KEGG definition of the pathway, purine biosynthesis is decreased in humans relative to apes in the brain as well as in other organs.
evidence: Supported by KEGG pathway analysis of metabolomic data

claim: A significant decrease in purine biosynthesis is seen in the three brain regions and not in muscle and kidney when using a more restrictive definition of purine biosynthesis.
source: If we focus on a more restrictive definition of purine biosynthesis (Marie et al., 2004), a significant decrease is seen in the three brain regions and not in muscle and kidney (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by metabolomic data shown in Figure 2

claim: Three metabolites (IMP, GMP and AMP) which individually have significantly lower concentrations in humans are products of de novo purine biosynthesis.
source: Further, three of the five metabolites, IMP, GMP and AMP, which individually have significantly lower concentrations in humans, are products of de novo purine biosynthesis.
evidence: Based on knowledge of purine biosynthesis pathway and metabolomic data

claim: Metabolites involved in purines biosynthesis have significantly lower concentrations in humans than in non-human primates in all three brain regions compared to metabolites in other metabolic pathways.
source: Taken together, metabolites involved in purines biosynthesis have significantly lower concentrations in humans than in non-human primates in all three brain regions than do metabolites in the other metabolic pathways, (Wilcoxon test, p=0.049 (PFC), p=0.002 (CB), p=0.001 (VC); Figure 2c).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of metabolomic data shown in Figure 2c

claim: Significantly lower concentrations of purine biosynthesis metabolites are found in humans compared to chimpanzees and macaques relative to other metabolic pathways when analyzing previously published metabolite data from the PFC.
source: Similarly, we find the significantly lower concentrations of purine biosynthesis metabolites in humans compared to chimpanzees and macaques relative to other metabolic pathways when analyzing previously published metabolite data from the PFC of three species (Kurochkin et al., 2019) (Wilcoxon test, p=0.019; Figure 2d).
evidence: Supported by reanalysis of published LC-MS data shown in Figure 2d

claim: Purine biosynthesis stands out as down-regulated in humans, seen in all tissues but particularly pronounced in the brain.
source: Thus, purine biosynthesis stands out as down-regulated in humans. This is seen in all tissues but is particularly pronounced in the brain.
evidence: Inferred from metabolomic data across multiple tissues

claim: ADSL catalyzes two reactions in de novo purine biosynthesis: cleaving SAICAR into AICAR and fumarate, and cleaving adenylosuccinate (S-AMP) into AMP and fumarate.
source: The enzyme adenylosuccinate lyase (ADSL) catalyzes two reactions in de novo purine biosynthesis (Figure 2a; Ciardo et al., 2001; Jaeken and Van den Berghe, 1984). First, it cleaves succinylaminoimidazole carboxamide ribotide (SAICAR) into aminoimidazole carboxamide ribotide (AICAR) and fumarate. Second, it cleaves adenylosuccinate (S-AMP) into adenosine monophosphate (AMP) and fumarate (Figure 2a).
evidence: Based on established knowledge of ADSL function and citations

claim: ADSL is a homotetrameric complex where three monomers contribute to each of the four active sites.
source: ADSL (Ariyananda et al., 2009) is a homotetrameric complex where three monomers contribute to each of the four active sites (Brosius and Colman, 2002).
evidence: Supported by citations to structural studies

claim: The gene encoding ADSL in humans is located on chromosome 22q13.1–13.2.
source: The gene encoding ADSL in humans is located on chromosome 22q13.1–13.2 and is one of only approximately one hundred protein-coding genes that carry substitutions inferred to change amino acids that are fixed or almost fixed in present-day humans but occur in their ancestral, ape-like state in the genomes of the closest extinct relatives of modern humans, Neandertals and Denisovans (Pääbo, 2014).
evidence: Based on genomic mapping data

claim: The compounds AMP, IMP, and GMP that are reduced in the three human brain regions analyzed are situated downstream of ADSL.
source: The compounds AMP, IMP, and GMP that are reduced in the three human brain regions analyzed are situated downstream of ADSL, consistent with the hypothesis that a change in ADSL may have caused the reduction in purine biosynthesis.
evidence: Based on knowledge of purine biosynthesis pathway and metabolomic data

claim: At position 428 adjacent to position 429, mice carry an arginine residue whereas primates carry a glutamine residue.
source: Adjacent to the amino acid of interest, at position 428, mice carry an arginine residue whereas primates carry a glutamine residue (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by sequence alignment data shown in Figure 3

claim: The two mutations (R428Q and A429V) segregate in Mendelian ratios in the humanized mice.
source: The two mutations segregate in Mendelian ratios in the mice, and animals heterozygous and homozygous for the two substitutions show no overt phenotypic difference to their wild-type littermates.
evidence: Supported by genetic analysis of mouse breeding

claim: Animals heterozygous and homozygous for the R428Q and A429V substitutions show no overt phenotypic difference to their wild-type littermates.
source: The two mutations segregate in Mendelian ratios in the mice, and animals heterozygous and homozygous for the two substitutions show no overt phenotypic difference to their wild-type littermates.
evidence: Based on phenotypic observation of mice

claim: In one-week-old pups, mean enzymatic activity was 5.4% to 57% higher in most tissues compared to adults and largely paralleled those of the adults.
source: In the pups (n = 10), mean enzymatic activity was 5.4% to 57% higher in most tissues and largely paralleled those of the adults (Figure 4a).
evidence: Supported by enzymatic activity measurements shown in Figure 4a

claim: ADSL activity was 41% lower in cerebellum and 11% lower in muscle in pups compared to adults.
source: Two exceptions were cerebellum and muscle, where ADSL activity was 41% and 11% lower in the pups than in the adults, respectively.
evidence: Supported by enzymatic activity measurements comparing pups and adults

claim: The number of putatively identified metabolites detected varied between 176 and 273 in adult mice and between 310 and 347 in young mice.
source: The number of putatively identified metabolites detected varied between 176 and 273 in the adult mice and between 310 and 347 in the young mice.
evidence: Supported by GC-MS metabolomic measurements

claim: An average of 280 (median = 273) metabolites were detected in at least 50% of the adult and young individuals in each of the nine tissues.
source: Among those, an average of 280 (median = 273) were detected in at least 50% of the adult and young individuals in each of the nine tissues (Supplementary files 7, 8).
evidence: Supported by GC-MS metabolomic measurements

claim: Among the organs analyzed, only the brain showed significant differences in metabolite concentrations between the wild type and humanized mice.
source: Among the organs analyzed, only the brain showed significant differences in metabolite concentrations between the wild type and humanized mice (Figure 5a).
evidence: Supported by statistical analysis of GC-MS metabolomic data shown in Figure 5a

claim: 45 metabolites showed marginally significant differences in the cerebral cortex of 1-week-old humanized mice compared to wild-type.
source: According to this test, 36 metabolites showed significant concentration differences in cerebellum of 12-week-old mice (permutation test, p=0.036) and 45 metabolites showed marginally significant differences in the cerebral cortex of 1-week-old mice (permutation test, p=0.081, Supplementary file 9).
evidence: Supported by GC-MS metabolomic measurements and statistical analysis

claim: The concentration differences detected in cerebellum of 12-week-old mice correlated with differences observed in cerebral cortex.
source: The concentration differences detected in cerebellum of the 12-week-old mice correlated with differences observed in cerebral cortex, even though differences in cortex did not pass the significance cut-off in the permutation test (Pearson correlation, r = 0.84, p<0.0001, n = 29; Figure 5—figure supplement 1a).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of metabolomic data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1a

claim: Concentration differences detected in cerebral cortex in one-week-old mice correlated with differences observed in cerebellum in the same mice.
source: Similarly, concentration differences detected in cerebral cortex in one-week-old mice correlated with differences observed in cerebellum in the same mice (Pearson correlation, r = 0.77, p<0.0001, n = 45; Figure 5—figure supplement 1b).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of metabolomic data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1b

claim: The concentration differences between wild type and humanized mice correlated between 1-week-old and 12-week-old mice both in cortex and in cerebellum.
source: The concentration differences between wild type and humanized mice furthermore correlated between the 1-week-old and 12-week-old mice both in cortex and in cerebellum (Pearson correlation, r = 0.49 and r = 0.52, p<0.008, n = 28 and n = 31, respectively; Figure 5—figure supplement 1e,f).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis of metabolomic data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1e,f

claim: The correlation between metabolic differences detected in brain and other tissues was weaker than correlations within brain tissues.
source: By contrast, the correlation between metabolic differences detected in brain and the other tissues was weaker (p<10−8 for brain tissues and p>10−4 for other tissues) (p<10−8; Figure 5—figure supplement 1c,d).
evidence: Supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1c,d

claim: In the humanized mouse, the effects of the substitutions in ADSL are seen in the cerebral cortex and cerebellum in both young and adult animals.
source: Thus, in the humanized mouse, the effects of the substitutions in ADSL are seen in the cerebral cortex and cerebellum in both young and adult animals.
evidence: Inferred from metabolomic data showing consistent effects across ages

claim: Seven metabolites in the purine biosynthesis pathway were detected in 1-week-old mice.
source: In the 1-week-old mice, we detected seven metabolites in the purine biosynthesis pathway.
evidence: Supported by GC-MS metabolomic measurements

claim: Five purine biosynthesis metabolites were present at lower concentrations in cerebral cortex and four at lower concentrations in cerebellum in 1-week-old humanized mice compared to wild-type.
source: Five of these were present at lower concentrations in the cerebral cortex in the humanized mice and four of these at lower concentrations in the cerebellum when compared to their wild-type litter mates (Figure 5b).
evidence: Supported by GC-MS metabolomic data shown in Figure 5b

claim: Several changes in concentrations of compounds in purine biosynthesis seen in the humanized mice recapitulate differences seen when the metabolomes of human brains are compared to the brains of chimpanzees and macaques.
source: Thus, several changes in concentrations of compounds in purine biosynthesis seen in the humanized mice recapitulate differences seen when the metabolomes of human brains are compared to the brains of chimpanzees and macaques.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of mouse and primate metabolomic data

claim: The effect on protein stability of the A429V substitution was not influenced by the presence or absence of the adjacent R428Q substitution at position 428.
source: The effect on the protein stability of the A429V substitution was not influenced by the presence or absence of the adjacent R428Q substitution at position 428.
evidence: Supported by circular dichroism measurements of different protein variants

claim: Both modern human and Neandertal versions of ADSL are able to rescue Chinese hamster ovary cells that lack ADSL activity.
source: To ensure that the two forms of the ADSL protein which differ only at position 429 in the protein are both enzymatically active in living cells we show that they both are able to rescue Chinese hamster ovary cells that lack ADSL activity (AdeI cells, Vliet et al., 2011; data not shown).
evidence: Supported by cell rescue experiments

claim: Circular dichroism spectra of both human and Neandertal protein versions exhibited predominantly alpha-helical characteristics.
source: In agreement with previous results (Van Laer et al., 2018), circular dichroism spectra of both protein versions exhibited predominantly alpha-helical characteristics (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by circular dichroism measurements and previous publication

claim: The conversion of SAMP to AMP is reduced approximately to the same extent (~2.4-fold) for the modern human and Neandertal-like forms of the enzyme when both substrates are present.
source: The conversion of SAMP to AMP is reduced approximately to the same extent (~2.4-fold, t-test, p=0.49) for the modern human and Neandertal-like forms of the enzyme when both substrates are present (Figure 7d).
evidence: Supported by enzyme kinetics measurements shown in Figure 7d

claim: The modern human enzyme produces less AICAR than the ancestral enzyme under physiological conditions.
source: This suggests that the modern human enzyme produces less AICAR than the ancestral enzyme under physiological conditions and may warrant further investigation.
evidence: Inferred from enzyme kinetics data with mixed substrates

claim: At 1.0125 M GdnHCl about 50% of the modern human version of ADSL was present as tetramers.
source: Figure 8b shows that at 1.0125 M GdnHCl about 50% of the modern human version of ADSL was present as tetramers whereas for the ancestral form this was the case at 1.125 M GdnHCl.
evidence: Supported by native gel electrophoresis measurements shown in Figure 8b

claim: Three independent cell lines with the V429A substitution in ADSL were isolated using CRISPR-Cas9.
source: We isolated three independent cell lines and we verified that the intended nucleotide substitution had occurred in each of them by sequencing a segment of the ADSL gene and excluded deletions of the target site by quantitative PCR (data not shown).
evidence: Supported by sequencing and qPCR data

claim: Six independent control cell lines were isolated that had been subjected to the CRISPR-Cas9 procedure but did not exhibit any mutation in the sequenced DNA segment.
source: We also isolated six independent lines that had been subjected to the CRISPR-Cas9 procedure but did not exhibit any mutation in the sequenced DNA segment.
evidence: Supported by sequencing data

claim: A total of 8849 metabolite peaks were detected in positive and negative mode LC-MS analysis of human cell lines.
source: A total of 8849 metabolite peaks were detected in positive and negative mode (Supplementary file 10).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS metabolomic measurements

claim: 1989 metabolite peaks were computationally annotated using KEGG.
source: Among them, 1989 were computationally annotated using KEGG.
evidence: Supported by computational annotation of LC-MS data

claim: Purine biosynthesis metabolites are present in lower amounts in wild-type human cells than in cells carrying the V429A substitution in ADSL.
source: These metabolites are present in lower amounts in the wild-type human cells than the cell carrying the V429A substitution in ADSL (Wilcoxon test, p=0.06; Figure 9b).
evidence: Supported by LC-MS metabolomic data shown in Figure 9b

claim: 1883 metabolite peaks differ significantly between human and chimpanzee wild-type cells.
source: Out of 1883 metabolite peaks that differ significantly (Wilcoxon test, BH-adjusted p<0.05) between the human and chimpanzee wild-type cells, four correspond to purine biosynthesis metabolites (guanosine, inosine, hypoxanthine, xanthine) and are present at lower levels in human cells compared to chimpanzee cells.
evidence: Supported by LC-MS metabolomic measurements and statistical analysis

claim: The A429V substitution is responsible for much or all of the difference in purine biosynthesis observed when human tissues are compared to ape and monkey tissues.
source: Thus, the A429V substitution is responsible for much or all of the difference in purine biosynthesis observed when human tissues are compared to ape and monkey tissues, indicating that this change in metabolism occurred in humans after their separation from the ancestor shared with Neandertals and Denisovans.
evidence: Inferred from combined data from humanized mice, ancestralized human cells, and primate comparisons

claim: This change in purine metabolism occurred in humans after their separation from the ancestor shared with Neandertals and Denisovans.
source: Thus, the A429V substitution is responsible for much or all of the difference in purine biosynthesis observed when human tissues are compared to ape and monkey tissues, indicating that this change in metabolism occurred in humans after their separation from the ancestor shared with Neandertals and Denisovans.
evidence: Inferred from the presence of the substitution in modern humans but not in Neandertals

claim: Although ADSL is expressed and functions in all tissues, the down-regulation of purine biosynthesis in humans relative to apes, and in humanized mice relative to wild-type mice, is most pronounced in the brain.
source: It is interesting that although ADSL is expressed and functions in all tissues, the down-regulation of purine biosynthesis in humans relative to apes, and in humanized mice relative to wild-type mice, is most pronounced in the brain.
evidence: Inferred from metabolomic and enzymatic data across tissues

claim: Mutations in humans that affect enzymes involved in purine metabolism have more pathological consequences in the nervous system than in other organs.
source: It is also interesting that mutations in humans that affect enzymes involved in purine metabolism have more pathological consequences in the nervous system than in other organs (Fumagalli et al., 2017; Micheli et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical studies

claim: No overt morphological or other brain-related phenotypes are observed in the mice humanized at positions 428 and 429.
source: Although no overt morphological or other brain-related phenotypes are observed in the mice humanized at pos. 428 and 429 (data not shown), it is thus possible that the A429V substitution in ADSL has contributed to human-specific changes in brain development and function.
evidence: Based on phenotypic observation of mice

claim: The number of metabolites annotated in the five tissues varied between 166 and 197, 160 and 209, and 145 and 192 in humans, chimpanzees, and macaques, respectively.
source: The number of metabolites annotated in the five tissues varied between 166 and 197, 160 and 209, and 145 and 192 in the three species, respectively (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Supported by CE-MS metabolomic measurements

claim: No metabolites differ significantly between macaques and chimpanzees but differ significantly in the same direction between humans and both other primates in skeletal muscle and kidney.
source: Whereas we find no such metabolites in skeletal muscle and kidney, we find metabolites peak intensities and thus concentrations differ in humans relative to the other two primates in two of the three parts of the brain analyzed.
evidence: Supported by CE-MS metabolomic measurements and statistical analysis

claim: Metabolite concentrations differ in humans relative to chimpanzees and macaques in two of the three parts of the brain analyzed.
source: Whereas we find no such metabolites in skeletal muscle and kidney, we find metabolites peak intensities and thus concentrations differ in humans relative to the other two primates in two of the three parts of the brain analyzed.
evidence: Supported by CE-MS metabolomic measurements

claim: No metabolites have lower concentrations in human cerebellum compared to chimpanzees and macaques.
source: In cerebellum, 22 metabolites have higher concentrations in humans whereas no metabolites have lower concentrations (Supplementary file 2).
evidence: Supported by CE-MS metabolomic measurements

claim: No metabolites have higher concentrations in human prefrontal cortex compared to chimpanzees and macaques.
source: In prefrontal cortex, we detected five metabolites with lower concentrations in humans and none with higher concentrations (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: Supported by CE-MS metabolomic measurements

claim: Between 4 and 11 pathways are associated with lower metabolite concentrations in the five tissues.
source: Between 4 and 11 pathways are associated with lower metabolite concentrations in the five tissues (Supplementary file 5).
evidence: Supported by KEGG pathway analysis of metabolomic data

claim: Amino acid and peptide metabolism make up one to five of the pathways with lower metabolite concentrations in different tissues.
source: Amino acid and peptide metabolism make up one to five of these pathways in the different tissues, suggesting that amino acid metabolism has changed in several ways in humans relative to the other primates.
evidence: Supported by KEGG pathway analysis of metabolomic data

claim: Amino acid metabolism has changed in several ways in humans relative to other primates.
source: Amino acid and peptide metabolism make up one to five of these pathways in the different tissues, suggesting that amino acid metabolism has changed in several ways in humans relative to the other primates.
evidence: Inferred from pathway analysis showing both increased and decreased metabolites in amino acid pathways

claim: Metabolites in arginine and proline metabolism are present in both higher and lower concentrations in humans, sometimes in the same tissues, suggesting that the flux through these pathways has changed.
source: For example, significant numbers of metabolites in arginine and proline metabolism are present in higher concentrations while other metabolites in the same pathways are present in lower concentrations, sometimes in the same tissues, suggesting that the flux through these pathways has changed.
evidence: Inferred from metabolomic data showing bidirectional changes in the same pathway

claim: Four of the six metabolites with lower concentrations in cerebellum in the humanized mice had lower concentrations in human cerebellum compared to other primates: AMP, GMP, inosine, and adenine.
source: Furthermore, four of the six metabolites with lower concentrations in cerebellum in the humanized mice had lower concentrations in human cerebellum compared to other primates: AMP, GMP, inosine, and adenine (Figures 2b and 5b).
evidence: Supported by comparison of metabolomic data from mice and primates shown in Figures 2b and 5b

claim: The six metabolites detected in 12-week-old mice were also detected in the primate brains.
source: The six metabolites detected in 12-week-old mice were also detected in the primate brains.
evidence: Supported by metabolomic measurements in both mice and primates

claim: Four of the six purine metabolites detected in primate brains had lower concentrations in the human brain.
source: Four of these had lower concentrations in the human brain, including AMP and GMP in prefrontal cortex, the visual cortex, and in cerebellum (binomial test, p=0.04).
evidence: Supported by CE-MS metabolomic measurements in primate brains

claim: AMP and GMP have lower concentrations in human prefrontal cortex, visual cortex, and cerebellum compared to other primates.
source: Four of these had lower concentrations in the human brain, including AMP and GMP in prefrontal cortex, the visual cortex, and in cerebellum (binomial test, p=0.04).
evidence: Supported by CE-MS metabolomic measurements
